questions.q: Which of the following shines only because it reflects the light that falls on it?
questions.a: The Moon. The Moon is non-luminous and only reflects the Sun's light; the star, flame and lightning emit their own light.
o: The Moon
The Pole Star
A burning candle flame
Lightning

questions.q: Which is the main source of natural light on the Earth?
questions.a: The Sun. The Sun emits its own light and is the main natural source on the Earth; the Moon and Venus only reflect sunlight.
o: The Sun
The Moon
Venus
Lightning

questions.q: Which statement about luminous objects is false?
questions.a: Every luminous object is a natural source of light. lectric lamps and candles are luminous but artificial, so 'every . natural' is false.
o: Every luminous object is a natural source of light.
Any object that emits its own light is called luminous.
A firefly flashing in the dark is a luminous object.
A burning candle in a room is a luminous object too.

questions.q: According to the chapter, fireflies use the light they produce to
questions.a: to communicate with one another. Jatin's grandparents explain that fireflies use light to communicate.
o: to communicate with one another
to reflect the moonlight back to the sky
to keep their bodies warm on cool nights
to make food by themselves at night

questions.q: A hill village earlier had hundreds of fireflies every summer night. Recently a resort has put up bright floodlights, thousands of tourists come every week and part of the forest was cleared. The firefly count has dropped. Which set of causes does the chapter give for such a decline?
questions.a: Light pollution, reduced forest cover and excessive tourism. The chapter names light pollution, reduced forest cover and excessive tourism.
o: Light pollution, reduced forest cover and excessive tourism
Heavy rain, fewer stars and brighter moonlight overhead
Strong sunlight, reflected moonlight and frequent lightning
Fewer LED lamps, dim headlights and cooler summer nights

questions.q: On the evening bus Keshav sees the Moon over the hills, the beams from the headlight lamps of passing buses, and the grey tarred road lit by those beams. Which choice names only the luminous objects?
questions.a: The headlight lamps only. Headlight lamps emit their own light; the Moon and the road only reflect light.
o: The headlight lamps only
The Moon and the headlight lamps
The Moon and the road
The road and the headlight lamps

questions.q:
Statement 1: Lightning and natural fire emit their own light, so they are natural luminous sources.
Statement 2: Electric lamps are artificial luminous objects.
Statement 3: The Moon is non-luminous because it only reflects the sunlight falling on it.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: 1, 2 and 3. Lightning and fire emit their own light, electric lamps are artificial sources, and the Moon only reflects sunlight; every statement is correct.
o: 1, 2 and 3
1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
1 and 3 only

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Venus is a non-luminous object even though it can be seen in the night sky.
Reason (R): Objects in our solar system other than the Sun shine only by reflecting sunlight.
questions.a: Both A and R are true and R explains A. Venus is seen because it reflects the Sun's light; it does not emit its own, which is why it is non-luminous.
o: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true

questions.q:
(a) Define luminous objects and give one natural and one artificial example.
(b) The Moon looks very bright at night. Why is it still not in this group?
questions.a: (a) Objects that emit their own light; natural: the Sun/stars/lightning/firefly; artificial: a candle, oil lamp or electric bulb. (b) The Moon does not emit light; it only reflects the sunlight falling on it, so it is non-luminous.
s: Part (a): definition with a natural and an artificial example

questions.q:
(a) State two advantages of LED lamps over traditional lamps.
(b) Which of these advantages lowers the electricity bill, and why?
questions.a: (a) Any two: consumes much less power, brighter, lasts longer. (b) Consuming much less power: the lamp uses less electricity, so the bill is lower.
s: Part (a): two advantages of LED lamps
Part (b): less power gives lower bill

questions.q: Differentiate between luminous and non-luminous objects, with one example of each.
questions.a: Luminous objects emit their own light (Sun, firefly); non-luminous objects do not emit light and are seen only when light falls on them and is reflected (Moon, mirror).
s: Difference: emit own light versus do not
One correct example of each kind

questions.q:
(a) Name two fuels that early humans used to make fire as artificial light.
(b) Is a flame burning these fuels luminous or non-luminous? Give the reason.
questions.a: (a) Any two of animal fat, oil, wax, gas. (b) Luminous: the flame emits its own light.
s: Part (a): two fuels from the chapter
Part (b): luminous because it emits its own light

questions.q:
(a) Name any two reasons for the decrease in the number of fireflies.
(b) Fireflies flash their light to communicate. Explain how bright floodlights near their forest can make this harder.
questions.a: (a) Any two of light pollution, reduced forest cover, excessive tourism. (b) Bright artificial light around them is light pollution, so their flashes are not easily noticed against it.
s: Part (b): light pollution hides their flashes

questions.q: Zoya says, 'A firefly is luminous but the Moon is not, although both are seen glowing in the dark.' Do you agree? Explain.
questions.a: Yes. A firefly emits its own light, so it is luminous. The Moon does not emit light; what we see is sunlight reflected by it, so it is non-luminous. Being visible in the dark does not decide it.

questions.q: A school wants to replace the traditional lamps in its hall with LED lamps. Give two benefits of this change and one thing the school must do when the LED lamps eventually fail.
questions.a: Benefits: LED lamps use much less power and last longer (also brighter, lower bills, better for environment). When they fail they must be disposed of or recycled properly, not thrown in the garbage.

questions.q: At a night fair, a stall has these things: a burning wax candle, a gas stove flame, a white wall lit by a torch, the Moon in the sky, an LED lamp and a shop mirror. Sort them into luminous and non-luminous and say how we are able to see the non-luminous ones.
questions.a: Luminous: candle, gas flame, LED lamp. Non-luminous: white wall, Moon, mirror. We see them only because they reflect light falling on them.
s: Non-luminous ones are seen by reflected light

questions.q: Trace how humans' sources of light changed over time, as the chapter describes, and then explain why the Moon is not a part of this list although it lights up the night.
questions.a: Early humans learnt to make fire, the first artificial light. They used different fuels such as animal fat, oil, wax and gas. With electricity came electric light sources, which now meet most lighting needs, and LED lamps are the modern ones. The Moon is non-luminous: it does not emit light, it reflects the Sun's light.
s: Fire as the earliest artificial light
Electric light sources and LED lamps

questions.q: A panchayat plans lighting for a three-day village mela near a forest where fireflies are seen every summer. Advise the panchayat on its lamp choice, the disposal of old lamps and the steps to protect fireflies, using ideas from the chapter.
questions.a: Choose LED lamps: much less power, brighter, last longer, lower bills. Dispose of or recycle failed lamps properly. Protect fireflies: avoid light pollution (do not flood the forest edge with bright light), keep the forest cover, and limit the crowds because excessive tourism reduces fireflies.
s: Recommends LED lamps with a reason
Proper disposal or recycling of old lamps
Avoid light pollution near the forest

questions.q:
Suresh runs a homestay in a Western Ghats village where guests come in summer to watch fireflies flash, see the Moon rise over the ridge and walk the forest path with small LED torches. He must choose a plan. Plan X: bright floodlights along the path and 200 guests a night at Rs 500 each. Plan Y: no path lights, torches only, and 30 guests a night at Rs 800 each.
(a) Which of the firefly, the Moon and the LED torch are luminous?
(b) Which two causes of firefly decline does Plan X raise?
(c) How much more does Plan X earn in one night than Plan Y?
(d) Which plan would you advise, and what is the trade-off?
questions.a: (a) Firefly and LED torch are luminous; the Moon is non-luminous. (b) Light pollution and excessive tourism. (c) Plan X earns 200 x 500 = Rs 1,00,000; Plan Y earns 30 x 800 = Rs 24,000; difference Rs 76,000. (d) Plan Y is the safer choice for the fireflies the guests come to see, though it earns Rs 76,000 less a night; an answer choosing X must still explain how fireflies will be protected.
s: Part (a): firefly and torch luminous, Moon not
Part (b): light pollution and excessive tourism
Part (d): justified choice weighing income against fireflies

questions.q:
Sunrise School has 60 traditional lamps in its corridors. Each costs Rs 50, and the school has found that during the time one LED lamp lasts it must buy 4 traditional lamps for the same place. An LED lamp costs Rs 150. This year the school has Rs 6,000 for lighting.
(a) Name two features of LED lamps from the chapter that favour them.
(b) For the whole corridor, what does the school spend on LED lamps and on traditional lamps over one LED lamp's lifetime?
(c) How many LED lamps can Rs 6,000 buy?
(d) Should the school buy 40 LED lamps now, or all 60 traditional lamps? State a decision and the duty that comes with the LED lamps.
questions.a: (a) Any two: consumes much less power, brighter, lasts longer. (b) LED: 60 x 150 = Rs 9,000; traditional: 60 x 50 x 4 = Rs 12,000. (c) 6000 / 150 = 40 lamps. (d) Buying 40 LED lamps costs Rs 6,000 now and saves money and power later, but 20 corridors stay on old lamps; buying 60 traditional lamps costs Rs 3,000 now but more over time. Either choice is accepted if reasoned; failed LED lamps must be disposed of or recycled properly.
s: Part (d): reasoned decision with disposal duty

questions.q: In Activity 11.1 a bright spot appears on the screen only when
questions.a: the three holes lie in one straight line. A spot is seen only when all three holes are in a line; moving one box removes it.
o: the three holes lie in one straight line
the three holes are at three different heights
the middle matchbox is moved a little to one side
the torch is placed behind the card screen

questions.q: In Activity 11.2 the candle flame can be seen
questions.a: through a straight pipe but not through a bent pipe. Light travels in a straight line, so the flame is visible only through the straight pipe.
o: through a straight pipe but not through a bent pipe
through a bent pipe but not through a straight pipe
through both the straight and the bent pipe
through neither a straight nor a bent pipe

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT a safe practice described in the chapter?
questions.a: Pointing a laser beam towards a friend to check it works. A laser beam must never be pointed at anyone's eyes because it can cause serious eye damage.
o: Pointing a laser beam towards a friend to check it works
Using only a low-power laser pointer for the activity
Using a laser only when a teacher is supervising the class
Lighting a candle only when an adult is present nearby

questions.q: A drop of milk is added to the water in the beaker before passing a laser beam through it in order to
questions.a: make the laser beam easily visible. The milk makes the beam visible so we can see that it follows a straight path.
o: make the laser beam easily visible
make the light travel faster
make the light bend around the beaker
make the water opaque

questions.q: Ishaan sets up three matchboxes with their holes exactly in a line at 4 cm above the table, but his torch lamp is at 6 cm and he sees no spot on the screen. What should he do to get the spot?
questions.a: Lower the torch so its lamp is at the height of the holes. Light travels in a straight line, so the lamp must be at the height of the holes; bending around the boxes is not what happens here.
o: Lower the torch so its lamp is at the height of the holes
Tilt the middle box so light can bend in through its hole
Take away the screen so light can reach the wall
Add a drop of milk to the torch to make light travel on

questions.q: Anil looks through a long hosepipe lying in a smooth curve across the lawn and tries to see a lighted lamp at the other end. He cannot see the lamp, but when a friend straightens the pipe he sees it. Which reason fits the chapter?
questions.a: Light travels in a straight line and cannot follow a curve. This is the bent-pipe activity: the flame is seen only when light can travel straight.
o: Light travels in a straight line and cannot follow a curve
Light cannot pass through any hollow tube, curved or straight
The lamp turns non-luminous when the pipe is bent in a curve
Light travels only through opaque materials like the pipe wall

questions.q:
Statement 1: A candle flame can always be seen through a pipe, whatever its shape, because light bends to follow the pipe.
Statement 2: A bright spot on the screen needs all three holes to be in one line.
Statement 3: A laser beam in water with a drop of milk follows a straight path.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: 2 and 3 only. The matchbox activity and the laser beam both show straight-line travel; the bent pipe stops the flame being seen, so the claim about any shape is false.
o: 2 and 3 only
1 and 2 only
1 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3

questions.q:
Assertion (A): A laser beam must never be pointed at anyone's eyes.
Reason (R): Light travels in a straight line.
questions.a: Both A and R are true but R does not explain A. The rule exists because the beam can cause serious eye damage, not because light travels straight.
o: Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
Both A and R are true and R explains A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true

questions.q:
(a) In Activity 11.1, what happens to the light spot when the middle matchbox is moved slightly to the side?
(b) What does this tell us about light?
questions.a: (a) The spot on the screen disappears. (b) Light travels in a straight line; the shifted hole is no longer in the path.
s: Part (b): light travels in a straight line

questions.q:
(a) State two precautions for using a laser in the water-and-milk activity.
(b) Why is a drop of milk added?
questions.a: (a) Use a low-power laser pointer, only under teachers' supervision, and never point at anyone's eyes (any two). (b) To make the beam easily visible so we see its straight path.

questions.q: State what is meant by 'light travels in a straight line' and give one evidence from the chapter.
questions.a: Light moves along straight paths and does not turn around obstacles in these activities. Evidence: a spot appears only when three holes are in one line; or the flame is seen through a straight but not a bent pipe.
s: Meaning: moves along a straight path

questions.q:
(a) The chapter says light can sometimes bend around corners. Does this contradict the bent pipe activity?
(b) What conclusion do we draw from the pipe activity at this grade?
questions.a: (a) No: bending around corners is a topic for higher grades and is not seen in this activity. (b) In this set-up, light travels in a straight line, so the flame is visible only through the straight pipe.
s: Part (a): no contradiction, learnt in higher grades

questions.q: Why must the three matchbox holes be at exactly the same position and height, and the torch lamp at the height of the holes, in Activity 11.1?
questions.a: Light travels in a straight line, so the torch, three holes and the screen spot must all lie along one straight line; any mismatch blocks the beam.
s: Light needs a straight line through all holes
Torch lamp at the same height or mismatch blocks light

questions.q: Neha reports a bright spot on the screen although the torch lamp and the first two holes are at 4 cm above the table and the third hole is at 6 cm. Show why this result cannot happen if light travels in a straight line.
questions.a: A beam from the lamp at 4 cm through two holes at 4 cm travels straight and horizontally at 4 cm. The third hole is at 6 cm, so the beam hits the box wall and is blocked; no spot can appear. The report must be wrong.
s: Straight beam stays at 4 cm height
Third hole at 6 cm is off the line
Beam blocked, so a spot is impossible

questions.q: The result of an experiment is: 'the candle flame could not be seen through the pipe'. Describe a set-up that gives this result and explain the cause. State the safety rule for the candle.
questions.a: Take a long flexible pipe, bend it and look for the candle flame at the other end; the flame is not seen because light travels in a straight line and cannot follow the bend. A lighted candle must be used under adult supervision only.

questions.q: Compare Activity 11.1 and Activity 11.2: give one thing they use in common, one difference in what is changed to stop the light, and the shared conclusion.
questions.a: Common: both use a light source (torch or candle) and look for light on the far side. Difference: Activity 11.1 moves a matchbox hole out of line; Activity 11.2 bends the pipe. Conclusion: light travels in a straight line.

questions.q: A student wants to test whether light travels in a straight line over a longer distance. She has a 2 m flexible pipe, a torch, a dark room and a wall. Plan the test: what she does with the straight pipe, what she does with the pipe bent, what she expects to see in each case, the conclusion, and one safety rule if she uses a candle instead of the torch.
questions.a: Straight pipe with the torch at one end: a patch of light is seen on the wall at the other end. Bent pipe: the patch is not seen, since light cannot follow the bend. Conclusion: light travels in a straight line. If a candle is used, it must be under adult supervision only.
s: Straight pipe set-up and expected result

questions.q: Aman says one activity is enough to prove that light travels in a straight line. Prisha says two or three different tests are better. Whose view do you support? Use the evidence of the chapter, name a third test, and give its precautions.
questions.a: Prisha: the chapter itself uses more than one test. Test 1: three matchboxes, spot lost if a hole is out of line. Test 2: flame seen through a straight pipe but not a bent one. A third test: laser beam in water with a drop of milk, which shows a straight beam. Precautions: low-power laser, only under teacher's supervision, never at anyone's eyes.
s: Supports Prisha with the chapter's practice
Third test: laser in milky water

questions.q:
A group has 20 minutes and plans two tests. Test 1 uses Activity 11.1 with the three matchboxes. In Trial A all three holes are in line at the lamp height and the screen is 30 cm away. Trial B is the same but the middle box is raised by 2 cm. Trial C is as Trial A, but the screen is moved to 60 cm. Test 2 would use a candle and a straight and a bent pipe, which needs an adult, who is free for only 10 minutes.
(a) Predict what is seen on the screen in Trial C.
(b) Predict what is seen in Trial B and give the reason.
(c) If the group adds two more matchboxes in the line, why does the test become harder to get right?
(d) Which plan should the group follow in 20 minutes, and why?
questions.a: (a) The spot is still seen, because the holes are still in line. (b) No spot, because the raised hole is out of line and light travels in a straight line. (c) Every hole must lie in the same line; one misplaced box blocks the beam. (d) Do Test 1 first, which needs no flame, then Test 2 within the adult's 10 minutes; a reasoned alternative is accepted.
s: Part (b): no spot, reason straight line
Part (c): all holes must be aligned

questions.q:
Rohit has a 1.5 m flexible pipe and wants to show his class that light travels in a straight line. He can use a lit candle 1 m away (an adult must be present) or a torch whose light he looks for on a wall at the other end (no flame, no adult needed). He will hold the pipe straight first and then bend it.
(a) What will he see through the straight pipe?
(b) What will he see once the pipe is bent?
(c) What does the change from (a) to (b) show about light?
(d) Which set-up should he choose if no adult is free, and what does he lose or gain?
questions.a: (a) The candle flame, or the torch's light patch, is seen. (b) It is not seen. (c) Light travels in a straight line and cannot follow the bend. (d) The torch set-up: no flame hazard and no adult needed, though the flame view shows the idea more vividly; the candle needs adult supervision only.
s: Part (a): source is seen through straight pipe
Part (b): not seen through bent pipe

questions.q: Tracing paper lets some light pass through but not all of it. Such a material is called
questions.a: translucent. Light passes partially through translucent materials.
o: translucent
transparent
opaque
luminous

questions.q: To observe a shadow we need
questions.a: a source of light, an opaque object and a screen. A shadow forms when an opaque object blocks light from a source falling on a screen.
o: a source of light, an opaque object and a screen
a luminous object, a plane mirror and a screen
a transparent object, a torch and no screen
an opaque object and a screen, but no source of light

questions.q: Which statement about shadows is NOT correct?
questions.a: Painting an opaque object red makes its shadow red. The colour of an opaque object does not change the colour of its shadow.
o: Painting an opaque object red makes its shadow red.
Opaque objects form darker shadows than translucent ones.
Translucent objects make lighter shadows than opaque ones.
Some transparent objects create faint shadows on a screen.

questions.q: In Activity 11.4 the torch is switched off while an opaque object stands in front of the screen. What happens to the shadow?
questions.a: No shadow can be seen. Without a source of light there is no light to block, so no shadow forms.
o: No shadow can be seen
The shadow becomes darker
The shadow becomes larger
The shadow becomes coloured

questions.q: Rekha places a thick wooden board and a sheet of tracing paper side by side in front of one torch, with a wall behind. She sees two patches on the wall, one behind each. Which description is right?
questions.a: The patch behind the board is darker than the patch behind the tracing paper. An opaque board blocks all light and gives a darker shadow; translucent tracing paper lets some light pass and gives a lighter one.
o: The patch behind the board is darker than the patch behind the tracing paper
The patch behind the tracing paper is darker, since it spreads the light about
Both patches are equally dark, since both objects are flat sheets
No patch forms behind the tracing paper, since it is not opaque

questions.q: At a science fair Priya cuts the same shape from red opaque card and from blue opaque card and holds each in turn in front of one torch with a white screen. What does she see?
questions.a: Both shadows look the same dark shape, not red or blue. Changing the colour of an opaque object does not change the colour of its shadow.
o: Both shadows look the same dark shape, not red or blue
A red shadow for the red card and a blue shadow for the blue card
A lighter shadow for the red card and a darker one for the blue card
No shadow for either, because coloured card is translucent

questions.q:
Statement 1: Light passes almost completely through transparent materials.
Statement 2: A translucent object forms a darker shadow than an opaque object.
Statement 3: Even some transparent objects can create faint shadows.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: 1 and 3 only. Transparent materials pass light almost fully and may still give a faint shadow; a translucent object passes some light, so its shadow is lighter, not darker.
o: 1 and 3 only
1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Opaque objects form darker shadows than translucent objects.
Reason (R): Opaque objects allow more light to pass through than translucent objects.
questions.a: A is true but R is false. A is true; R is false because opaque objects allow no light to pass, which is why their shadows are darker.
o: A is true but R is false
Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is false but R is true

questions.q:
Match the materials and terms in Column A with the descriptions in Column B.
Column A: 1 Transparent  2 Translucent  3 Opaque  4 Luminous
Column B: a Blocks light completely  b Emits its own light  c Lets light pass almost completely  d Lets light pass partially
questions.a: 1-c, 2-d, 3-a, 4-b. Transparent passes light almost completely, translucent partly, opaque none, luminous emits.

questions.q:
(a) Classify clear window glass, tracing paper and cardboard as transparent, translucent or opaque.
(b) Which of the three will form the darkest shadow, and why?
questions.a: (a) Clear window glass: transparent; tracing paper: translucent; cardboard: opaque. (b) Cardboard, as it blocks light completely.
s: Part (b): opaque cardboard blocks light fully

questions.q: Define a shadow and name the three things needed to observe it.
questions.a: A shadow is the dark patch where light does not reach, formed when an object blocks light. Needed: a source of light, an opaque object and a screen.

questions.q:
(a) What happens to the shadow if the screen is removed, and if the object is removed?
(b) Which of the three requirements for a shadow is taken away in each case?
questions.a: (a) With no screen there is nothing on which to see the shadow, and with no object light is not blocked, so no shadow either way. (b) Removing the screen removes the screen; removing the object removes the opaque object.
s: Part (a): no shadow in both cases
Part (b): requirement removed in each case

questions.q: Differentiate between a transparent and a translucent material on the basis of the light passing through them and the shadow they form. Give one example of each.
questions.a: Transparent lets light pass almost completely and gives at most a faint shadow (clear glass); translucent lets light pass partially and makes a lighter shadow (tracing paper).
s: Difference in light passing and shadow

questions.q:
(a) Name two shadow puppetry styles from different states mentioned in the chapter.
(b) In a shadow play, what acts as the light source, the opaque object and the screen?
questions.a: (a) Any two: Tholu Bommalata (Andhra Pradesh), Togalu Gombeyaata (Karnataka), Keelu Bomme, Charma Bahuli Natya, Ravana Chhaya, Tholpavakoothu, Bommalattam. (b) Lamp/light is the source, the flat cut-out puppet the opaque object, the screen is where the shadow is seen.

questions.q: Ravi says, 'A sheet of tracing paper and a wooden board both make shadows, but the tracing paper's shadow is lighter because it lets some light through.' Do you agree? Explain, and say what you expect from clear glass.
questions.a: Yes. Tracing paper is translucent and passes light partially, so it makes a lighter shadow; the wooden board is opaque and makes a darker one. Clear glass is transparent and may give only a faint shadow.
s: Translucent passes partial light, lighter shadow
Clear glass: faint shadow at most

questions.q: A teacher places a wooden board, a steel plate, tracing paper and clear glass one at a time between a torch and a screen. Classify each, and arrange them from the darkest shadow to the faintest.
questions.a: Wooden board and steel plate: opaque; tracing paper: translucent; clear glass: transparent. Order: board and steel plate (darkest), then tracing paper (lighter), then clear glass (faintest).

questions.q: A student holds an opaque board in front of a torch that is switched on, and a wall is nearby, yet no shadow can be seen on the wall. Write two different situations that could explain this, and say what each shows about the needs of a shadow.
questions.a: Any two: (1) the wall (screen) lies outside the part of the space the light reaches, so nothing receives the shadow; (2) the torch is pointed away so its light never reaches the board; (3) the board is placed where its blocked patch does not fall on the wall. Each shows that a source, an opaque object and a screen must be placed suitably relative to one another.
s: First situation consistent with a lit torch
Second situation consistent with a lit torch
Link to needs and positions for a shadow

questions.q: Ishaan wants to find out whether the colour of an opaque cut-out changes the colour of its shadow, and whether the position of the lamp matters. Plan the experiment: what he changes, what he keeps the same, what he expects to observe, and the conclusions.
questions.a: He uses one lamp, one screen and two cut-outs of the same shape, one red and one green, keeping lamp and screen fixed and changing only the colour. Expected: both shadows are the same dark patch, so colour of an opaque object does not change its shadow's colour. Then he moves the lamp or the cut-out and notes that shape, size and sharpness of the shadow change with the positions of object, source and screen. Conclusions: colour has no effect; position does.
s: Colour is the one thing changed, other things fixed
Second test: moves lamp or object
Observes size, shape or sharpness change

questions.q: Compare transparent, translucent and opaque materials in terms of how much light passes and what kind of shadow they form. Then explain, using the chapter, why the shadow of your hand on a wall looks different when the hand is held close to the wall and when it is held close to the lamp.
questions.a: Transparent: almost completely, faint shadow. Translucent: partially, lighter shadow. Opaque: none, darker shadow. The shape, size and sharpness of a shadow depend on the position of the object relative to the light source and the screen, so moving the hand nearer the wall or the lamp changes its shadow.
s: Position of object, source and screen matter
Applies to the hand near the wall versus near the lamp

questions.q:
A shadow-puppet troupe stages a show with a lamp behind a cloth screen and flat figures moved between them. The director has three sheets for the figures: thick card, thin tracing sheet and clear plastic. She wants a bold dark hero, a pale ghost, and she paints the hero's card red in one scene and green in another.
(a) Which sheet will give the darkest outline on the screen, and why?
(b) What colour will the hero's shadow have in the red and the green scenes?
(c) What will the thin tracing sheet and the clear plastic each give?
(d) The hall is large and the back rows must still see the ghost. Which sheet would you pick for the ghost, and what is the risk?
questions.a: (a) Thick card: it is opaque and blocks the light fully. (b) The same dark shadow in both scenes; the colour of an opaque object does not change the colour of its shadow. (c) Tracing sheet: a lighter shadow; clear plastic: at most a faint shadow. (d) The tracing sheet gives a pale but visible ghost; the risk is that it may look too faint from the back rows, so a brighter lamp or closer screen may be needed. Clear plastic is likely too faint.

questions.q:
Ananya tests four sheets P, Q, R and S one at a time between a torch and a screen. With P, no light reaches the screen. With Q, a dim patch of light reaches it. With R, almost all the light reaches the screen. With S, only a very faint glow reaches it, fainter than with Q. The school wants a window blind for a hall that hides what is inside but still lets in some daylight.
(a) Classify P, Q, R and S.
(b) Arrange the four from the darkest shadow to the faintest.
(c) Will R form a shadow at all? Explain.
(d) Which sheet would you choose for the blind, Q or S, and what do you give up?
questions.a: (a) P opaque; Q and S translucent; R transparent. (b) P darkest, then S, then Q, then R faintest. (c) Yes, a faint one; some transparent objects can create faint shadows. (d) Q lets in more daylight but hides less; S hides more but makes the hall dimmer. Either is accepted if the trade-off is stated; P would block all light and R would not hide the room.

questions.q: The change in the direction of light when it falls on a mirror is called
questions.a: reflection of light. This is the definition of reflection of light.
o: reflection of light
formation of a shadow
lateral inversion
luminosity

questions.q: Which of the following could be used to redirect sunlight onto a shaded wall?
questions.a: A shiny flat steel plate. A shiny flat surface changes the direction of light; the others transmit or absorb light.
o: A shiny flat steel plate
A sheet of tracing paper
A black cardboard sheet
A piece of thick cloth

questions.q: Which statement about a plane mirror is false?
questions.a: After reflection, light no longer moves in straight lines. ight always travels in straight lines, changing direction only at the mirror.
o: After reflection, light no longer moves in straight lines.
A plane mirror is a flat mirror and not a curved one.
Tilting the mirror changes the place where the spot falls.
The Moon shines by reflecting the sunlight falling on it.

questions.q: The Aranmula Kannadi, made in Kerala for centuries, is
questions.a: a metal surface mirror. The chapter calls it a unique metal surface mirror.
o: a metal surface mirror
a glass lens used for reading
a pinhole camera
a lamp burning oil

questions.q: In Activity 11.6 Radha makes a thin beam of light along white paper using a comb with one slit and a torch. When she places a plane mirror in the beam's path, the beam leaves the mirror along a new direction. Which idea does this show?
questions.a: Reflection of light by the mirror. The mirror changes the direction of the beam, which is reflection.
o: Reflection of light by the mirror
Formation of a shadow by the mirror
Light bending because the paper is white
The mirror giving out its own light

questions.q: Kabir throws a spot of sunlight on a wall using a steel plate. When he tilts the plate slightly upwards, the spot moves higher on the wall. What does this show?
questions.a: Tilting changes the direction of reflected light, which still travels straight. Tilting the mirror changes the position of the spot; light still travels in straight lines.
o: Tilting changes the direction of reflected light, which still travels straight
The plate makes the light travel faster when it is tilted upwards by hand and held
Light bends in a smooth curve as the plate is moved up and then moved down
The plate produces extra light of its own whenever it is tilted by a person

questions.q:
Statement 1: A plane mirror is a flat mirror, not curved.
Statement 2: We see our face in a mirror due to reflection of light.
Statement 3: Only a glass mirror can reflect light; a shiny steel plate cannot.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: 1 and 2 only. A shiny steel plate also reflects light, so the claim that only a glass mirror can is false.
o: 1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
1 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3

questions.q:
Assertion (A): A shiny steel plate can throw a spot of sunlight onto a wall.
Reason (R): Light travels in straight lines.
questions.a: Both A and R are true but R does not explain A. Both are true, but the spot appears because a shiny surface changes the direction of light (reflection); straight-line travel alone does not explain it.
o: Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
Both A and R are true and R explains A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true

questions.q:
(a) Define reflection of light.
(b) In Activity 11.6, what shows that reflection has taken place?
questions.a: (a) The change in direction of light by a mirror. (b) The path of the thin light beam changes after it falls on the plane mirror.

questions.q:
(a) How can you send sunlight onto a wall that the Sun does not directly reach, using a steel plate?
(b) What happens to the light spot if you tilt the plate?
questions.a: (a) Hold the shiny flat plate in sunlight and turn it so the light falls on the wall. (b) The spot changes its position on the wall.
s: Part (a): plate turned to redirect sunlight
Part (b): spot changes position when tilted

questions.q: In the mirror Rani can see her own face. Is this due to reflection of light? Explain in a line.
questions.a: Yes. Light falling on the face is sent back by the mirror, which changes its direction (reflection), so she sees her face.
s: Mirror changes the direction of light to the eye

questions.q:
(a) Where does moonlight come from?
(b) Is the Moon a luminous object? Give the reason using your answer to (a).
questions.a: (a) It is sunlight falling on the Moon and reflected by it. (b) No, it is non-luminous: it only reflects light and does not emit its own.

questions.q:
(a) How were mirrors made before glass mirrors?
(b) Why did the making of metal mirrors gradually decline, according to the chapter?
questions.a: (a) By polishing stone or metal. (b) When glass mirrors started being made, the art of making metal mirrors gradually got lost.

questions.q: Tarun says, 'The sunlight spot on the wall comes from the steel plate itself, so the plate is a luminous object.' Do you agree? Explain.
questions.a: No. The plate only changes the direction of sunlight falling on it (reflection); it does not emit its own light. So it is non-luminous.
s: Does not emit its own light, hence non-luminous

questions.q: Kabir wants to send a bright flash of sunlight to a friend standing at the far end of the school ground, using a shiny steel plate. Describe how he should use the plate, what he should do if the flash falls short of his friend, and what his friend would see.
questions.a: He holds the plate in sunlight and turns it so the reflected light travels towards his friend. If the flash falls short he tilts the plate to change the position of the spot. His friend sees a bright spot of light, because the plate has changed the direction of sunlight (reflection).
s: Turns the plate to direct sunlight at his friend
Tilts it to adjust the spot

questions.q: Describe one everyday situation where we use reflection by a plane mirror to see something, and say how the idea of reflection explains it.
questions.a: Example: looking at one's face in a mirror, or the rear-view mirror of a vehicle. Light from the object is sent by the mirror towards the eye, because the mirror changes the direction of light (reflection).
s: Light changed in direction by the mirror

questions.q: Compare Activity 11.5 and Activity 11.6: in each, name the light source, the reflecting surface and what shows that the light's direction has changed.
questions.a: Activity 11.5: Sun is the source, the shiny steel plate or mirror is the surface, and the spot on the wall shows the change. Activity 11.6: the torch is the source, the plane mirror is the surface, and the change in path of the thin beam on white paper shows it.
s: Evidence of changed direction for both

questions.q: Rekha's father runs a roadside shop whose signboard stays in shade the whole day while the shop opposite is in sunlight. Suggest how a flat shiny steel sheet or plane mirror could be used to light the signboard, how the spot is kept on the board as the Sun's light changes, and what stays true about the light's path.
questions.a: Place the sheet or mirror in the sunlight and turn it so the sunlight is directed on to the signboard. As the sunlight changes direction, tilt the sheet to move the spot back onto the board. Light still travels in straight lines to the sheet and from it; only its direction is changed by reflection. A shiny flat surface is needed.
s: Uses sunlight on a shiny flat surface
Turns it to direct light on to the board
Tilts to keep the spot on the board
Light still travels in straight lines

questions.q: Plan an investigation into how the position of a sunlight spot on a wall depends on the tilt of a plane mirror. Say what you will keep fixed, what you will change, what you will observe, what you conclude about the path of light, and one thing you will compare with a shadow experiment.
questions.a: Keep the Sun side, the wall and the mirror's place fixed; change only the tilt of the mirror, a little at a time. Observe that the spot moves to a new position for each tilt. Conclusion: the mirror changes the direction of light (reflection) while light still travels in straight lines. Comparison: in a shadow the object blocks light, but here the mirror sends the light on in a new direction.
s: Keeps place of mirror and wall fixed

questions.q:
The village library has a reading corner that never gets direct sunlight. Rohan will use a plane mirror placed outside the window. Plan P: fix the mirror on a wooden stand and leave it in place all day. Plan Q: let a volunteer hold the mirror and re-tilt it every half hour.
(a) What is the change in direction of light by the mirror called?
(b) How can Rohan move the light spot higher on the wall?
(c) By afternoon, with a fixed mirror, the spot slides off the corner. What does this tell you about the effect of tilt and direction on the spot?
(d) Which option would you advise, and what does each cost or gain?
questions.a: (a) Reflection of light. (b) Tilt the mirror. (c) The spot's position depends on how the mirror is tilted and on the direction of the incoming light, so it moves when either changes. (d) Plan Q keeps the spot in the corner but needs a volunteer's time; Plan P needs no one but the spot drifts away. A reasoned choice or a combined plan is accepted.
s: Part (c): spot depends on tilt and incoming direction
Part (d): reasoned choice with cost and gain

questions.q:
At a museum in Kerala a school group sees a glass mirror and the Aranmula Kannadi side by side. The guide says both help a visitor see her face, that the art of making one kind of mirror gradually got lost, and that the trust running the museum must decide between paying for workshops to keep the old craft alive or spending the money on more glass mirrors for visitors.
(a) Which of the two is a metal surface mirror, and which is it that the art is about?
(b) Why did the art of making this kind of mirror gradually get lost?
(c) How does either mirror let a visitor see her face?
(d) Which would you advise the trust to fund, and what does each choice gain or lose?
questions.a: (a) The Aranmula Kannadi is the metal surface mirror made for centuries in Kerala. (b) Glass mirrors started being made. (c) By reflection: the mirror changes the direction of light from her face back to her eyes. (d) Workshops keep a craft that survives only in Kerala but serve fewer visitors; glass mirrors serve more visitors but do nothing for the craft. A reasoned choice is accepted.
s: Part (a): Kannadi is the metal surface mirror
Part (d): reasoned choice weighing gain and loss

questions.q: The image formed by a plane mirror is
questions.a: erect, the same size as the object, and cannot be obtained on a screen. These are the properties given in the chapter; the others mix in pinhole camera features or wrong sizes.
o: erect, the same size as the object, and cannot be obtained on a screen
inverted, the same size as the object, and can be obtained on a screen
erect, smaller than the object, and can be obtained on a screen
upside down, laterally inverted and seen behind the mirror

questions.q: A plane mirror forms the image of an object at a distance behind the mirror that is
questions.a: equal to the object distance. The image appears as far behind the mirror as the object is in front of it.
o: equal to the object distance
double the distance of the object in front of it
half the distance of the object in front of it
zero, as the image lies right on the mirror

questions.q: The perceived left-right reversal in the image formed by a plane mirror is called
questions.a: lateral inversion. In the image, left appears right and right appears left: lateral inversion.
o: lateral inversion
reflection of light
an erect image
a shadow

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT true of the image formed in a plane mirror?
questions.a: It can be caught on a screen placed behind it. e image cannot be obtained on a screen, whether the screen is behind or in front of the mirror.
o: It can be caught on a screen placed behind it.
It is erect, right side up and not upside down.
It is exactly the same size as the object is.
It is laterally inverted, with left shown as right.

questions.q: Meena stands 3 m in front of a plane mirror and then walks away until she is 5 m from it. By how much has the distance between Meena and her image increased?
questions.a: 4 m. Before: 3 + 3 = 6 m. After: 5 + 5 = 10 m. Increase 4 m. A 2 m answer forgets that the image moves back too; 10 m and 6 m are the new and old separations, not the increase.
o: 4 m
2 m
6 m

questions.q: Aman wears his wrist watch on his left wrist and stands facing a plane mirror. On which wrist does the watch appear to be in his image, and why?
questions.a: On the right wrist of the image, because left appears right. Lateral inversion makes left appear right; the image is erect and not upside down.
o: On the right wrist of the image, because left appears right
On the left wrist of the image, because the image is the same size
On the right wrist, because the image is upside down
On the left wrist, because the image is erect

questions.q:
Statement 1: The image in a plane mirror becomes smaller as the object moves farther from the mirror.
Statement 2: The image in a plane mirror cannot be obtained on a screen, whether the screen is behind or in front of the mirror.
Statement 3: The letters T and O look identical to themselves in a plane mirror.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: 2 and 3 only. The image has the same size as the object at every position, so the claim about shrinking is false; the screen and letter statements follow the chapter.
o: 2 and 3 only
1 and 2 only
1 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3

questions.q:
Assertion (A): A plane mirror image can be caught on a screen held in front of the mirror.
Reason (R): The image seen in a plane mirror appears to be behind the mirror.
questions.a: A is false but R is true. A is false because the image cannot be obtained on a screen at all; R is true.
o: A is false but R is true
Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false

questions.q:
Match the terms in Column A with the statements in Column B.
Column A: 1 Lateral inversion  2 Erect image  3 Image distance  4 Screen kept behind a plane mirror
Column B: a Same as the object distance  b Left appears right and right appears left  c Upright  d Image cannot be obtained on it
questions.a: 1-b, 2-c, 3-a, 4-d. Lateral inversion is the left-right swap; erect is upright; image distance equals object distance; no image forms on the screen.

questions.q:
(a) List three properties of the image formed by a plane mirror.
(b) Which property makes your left hand appear as the right hand in the image?
questions.a: (a) Any three: same size, erect, cannot be obtained on a screen, appears behind the mirror as far as the object is in front, laterally inverted. (b) Lateral inversion.

questions.q:
Ria stands 2.5 m in front of a plane mirror.
(a) How far behind the mirror is her image?
(b) How far is she from her image?
s: Part (b): 5.0 m between her and the image

questions.q: Why is the word AMBULANCE written laterally inverted on the front of an ambulance?
questions.a: In the rear-view mirror of the vehicle ahead, lateral inversion reverses the writing again, so the word reads correctly (AMBULANCE) to the driver in front.
s: Mirror image reverses left and right
Word reads correctly in the rear-view mirror

questions.q:
(a) Define lateral inversion.
(b) Would the lateral inversion of the letters T, O and R be equally easy to notice in a plane mirror? Explain.
questions.a: (a) The perceived left-right reversal in the image formed by a plane mirror. (b) No: T and O look identical to themselves, so the reversal cannot be noticed, but R looks reversed.
s: Part (b): T and O look the same, R does not

questions.q: Differentiate between an object and its image in a plane mirror on the basis of position and whether it can be caught on a screen.
questions.a: The object stands in front of the mirror; the image appears behind the mirror. The image cannot be obtained on a screen, whether placed behind or in front of the mirror.
s: Position: in front versus behind the mirror

questions.q: Kavya says, 'When I walk away from a plane mirror my image stays the same size, and it always appears as far behind the mirror as I am in front.' Do you agree? Explain.
questions.a: Yes. The image formed by a plane mirror is the same size as the object at every position, and it appears as far behind the mirror as the object is in front of it, so the distance moves with her.

questions.q: Sneha stands 2 m in front of a plane mirror. Her friend says the image is 3 m behind the mirror. Show that this cannot be right.
questions.a: The image appears as far behind the mirror as the object is in front. Sneha is 2 m in front, so the image is 2 m behind, not 3 m. The distance between them would be 4 m, not 5 m.
s: Applies to 2 m: image at 2 m

questions.q: Write a secret message for a friend that can be read only by holding it in front of a plane mirror. Say how you would write it and what the friend will see in the mirror.
questions.a: Write the words reversed from left to right (laterally inverted), for example write the letters in reverse order with each letter reversed. In the mirror, lateral inversion swaps left and right again, so the friend sees the message reading correctly.
s: Mirror reverses left and right again
Message appears correct in the image

questions.q: Compare an object and its image in a plane mirror in terms of size, erectness and left-right. State what is the same and what changes.
questions.a: Size: same. Erect: yes, upright like the object. Left-right: reversed. Same: size and erectness; changes: left-right, i.e. lateral inversion.

questions.q: Anu says that if she stands twice as far from a plane mirror, her image will also be twice as far behind it and will look twice as small. Rohit says the image stays the same size. Make a table for her standing 1 m, 2 m and 3 m from the mirror, giving the distance of the image behind the mirror and the distance between her and the image, and decide who is right.
questions.a: At 1 m: image 1 m behind, separation 2 m. At 2 m: image 2 m behind, separation 4 m. At 3 m: image 3 m behind, separation 6 m. Anu is right that the image distance doubles when she stands twice as far. She is wrong that it looks smaller: the image has the same size as the object at all positions, so Rohit is right about size.
s: Image distance at 1 m, 2 m, 3 m

questions.q: Explain the use of lateral inversion on ambulances: describe what happens to the lettering in the rear-view mirror, what would happen if it were written normally, and why the writing is not upside down in the mirror.
questions.a: A plane mirror image has left and right interchanged. Letters painted laterally inverted are re-reversed in the rear-view mirror and read correctly. If written normally, the mirror would show reversed letters that are hard to read. The image in a plane mirror is erect, so it is not upside down; only left and right swap.
s: Mirror image is erect, not upside down

questions.q:
In a dance class Kavya stands 1.2 m in front of the large plane mirror on the studio wall. She then moves away from the mirror by 0.8 m. The teacher wants the dancers to check a move called 'left arm up' by looking in the mirror.
(a) How far behind the mirror is her image at first?
(b) What is the distance between Kavya and her image at first?
(c) After she moves away by 0.8 m, what is the distance between her and her image?
(d) Should the dancers use the mirror to check the move? Decide and explain which arm of the image they should expect to see raised.
questions.a: (a) 1.2 m. (b) 1.2 + 1.2 = 2.4 m. (c) She is 2.0 m from the mirror, so 2.0 + 2.0 = 4.0 m. (d) Yes, if they remember lateral inversion: the left arm they raise appears as the right arm of the image, so they should expect the image's right arm; a reasoned 'no' that suggests checking by a classmate instead is also accepted.

questions.q:
The school drama club will place a card at the back of the stage that actors read by looking at its image in a large plane mirror, while the audience in front can read the card directly. The club uses a card with the two letters T and O, and later a card with a longer word.
(a) How will the image of the card TO read in the mirror?
(b) Which property of the image explains this?
(c) How should the club write a card so that its image reads TO?
(d) The audience must read the card directly and the actors must read its image. Should the club write one card or two, and how? Justify.
questions.a: (a) The letters look identical but their order is reversed: it reads OT. (b) Lateral inversion: left and right appear interchanged. (c) Write OT, which becomes TO in the image. (d) Two cards: one written normally for the audience and one written laterally inverted for the actors, since a single card cannot read correctly both directly and in the mirror; a single card with clear justification of the choice is also accepted.
s: Part (d): reasoned decision on one or two cards

questions.q: The image formed on the screen of a pinhole camera is
questions.a: inverted (upside down). In Activity 11.9 the image of the candle flame is upside down.
o: inverted (upside down)
erect and laterally inverted
erect and the same as the object
not formed at all

questions.q: A simple periscope is made by placing
questions.a: two plane mirrors in a Z-shaped box. The chapter's periscope uses two plane mirrors in a Z-shaped box; three strips in a triangle make a kaleidoscope.
o: two plane mirrors in a Z-shaped box
three plane mirror strips in a triangle
a tiny hole and a screen in two boxes
one curved mirror in a straight tube

questions.q: Which device uses three plane mirror strips joined in a triangle, with coloured bangle pieces?
questions.a: A kaleidoscope. That is the construction of the kaleidoscope.
o: A kaleidoscope
A periscope
A pinhole camera
A plane mirror with stand

questions.q: Which statement about a kaleidoscope is false?
questions.a: It shows the same pattern every time it is turned. A different pattern is seen every time the kaleidoscope is turned.
o: It shows the same pattern every time it is turned.
It is made using three plane mirror strips.
Designers and artists use it to get new ideas.
Reflections of reflections make multiple images in it.

questions.q: A soldier in a bunker wants to see what is happening outside without raising his head above the wall. Which device from the chapter helps, and what does it use?
questions.a: A periscope, using reflection from two plane mirrors. A periscope's two mirrors let us see objects not visible directly.
o: A periscope, using reflection from two plane mirrors
A kaleidoscope, using three plane mirror strips
A pinhole camera, using a tiny hole and a screen
A single plane mirror, using only the idea of lateral inversion

questions.q: Aryan points his sliding pinhole camera at a tall building in bright sunlight and moves the smaller box until an image appears on the tracing paper. What does he see?
questions.a: An upside-down image of the building. A pinhole camera forms an inverted image; the left-right reversal without inversion belongs to a plane mirror.
o: An upside-down image of the building
An upright image of the building
A left-right reversed but upright image
No image, because the hole is tiny

questions.q: Mira turns a kaleidoscope slowly. The same bangle pieces are inside, yet she sees a new pattern every time. Which reason fits the chapter?
questions.a: Many images from reflections of reflections that change as the pieces move. Three mirrors give multiple images from reflections of reflections.
o: Many images from reflections of reflections that change as the pieces move
Light inside the tube bends in a curve and makes new coloured pieces appear
The tracing paper changes the colour of the bangle pieces whenever it is turned
The tube works as a pinhole camera that turns all the pieces upside down

questions.q:
Statement 1: A pinhole camera forms an inverted image on a screen.
Statement 2: The image in a plane mirror is also upside down.
Statement 3: A periscope uses two plane mirrors to let us see objects not directly visible.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: 1 and 3 only. A plane mirror image is laterally inverted but not upside down, so the claim about it being upside down is false.
o: 1 and 3 only
1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3

questions.q:
Assertion (A): A kaleidoscope with three mirrors gives a new pattern every time it is turned.
Reason (R): Reflections of reflections in the mirrors produce multiple images.
questions.a: Both A and R are true and R explains A. Both are true and multiple images from reflections of reflections explain the changing pattern.
o: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true

questions.q:
Match the devices in Column A with their features in Column B.
Column A: 1 Periscope  2 Kaleidoscope  3 Pinhole camera  4 Plane mirror
Column B: a Forms an inverted image on a screen  b Two mirrors in a Z-shaped box  c Three mirror strips giving multiple images  d Gives an erect, laterally inverted image
questions.a: 1-b, 2-c, 3-a, 4-d. Periscope: two mirrors; kaleidoscope: three strips; pinhole camera: inverted image; plane mirror: erect, laterally inverted.

questions.q:
(a) What is a pinhole camera?
(b) How does the image on its screen differ from the image seen in a plane mirror?
questions.a: (a) A device in which light rays from an object pass through a tiny hole and form an image on a screen. (b) The pinhole image is inverted (upside down) and falls on a screen; the plane mirror image is erect, laterally inverted and cannot be obtained on a screen.
s: Part (b): inverted versus erect and laterally inverted

questions.q:
(a) In the sliding pinhole camera, which part is moved to focus the image and what is used as the screen?
(b) What kind of object and light is used for viewing?
questions.a: (a) The smaller box is moved forward or backward; tracing paper is the screen. (b) A distant object (like a tree or building) in bright sunlight.
s: Part (a): smaller box moved, tracing paper screen
Part (b): distant object in bright sunlight

questions.q:
(a) Where are the two plane mirrors placed in a periscope?
(b) How do the two mirrors help a soldier in a bunker see outside?
questions.a: (a) In a Z-shaped box, one at each bend. (b) Reflection from the two mirrors lets him see objects that are not directly visible.
s: Part (a): two mirrors in Z-shaped box
Part (b): reflection from both mirrors shows hidden objects

questions.q:
(a) Which device from this section depends on reflection from mirrors, a periscope or a pinhole camera?
(b) In the other device, what lets an image form on the screen?
questions.a: (a) The periscope. (b) Light rays from the object passing through the tiny hole form the image on the screen.
s: Part (b): rays through the tiny hole form the image

questions.q:
(a) What materials are put at the end of a kaleidoscope tube to make patterns?
(b) Why does turning the tube give a different pattern each time?
questions.a: (a) Broken pieces of coloured bangles or beads, on a transparent sheet covered with tracing paper. (b) The pieces move and the three mirrors form multiple images (reflections of reflections), so a new pattern appears.
s: Part (a): coloured bangle pieces or beads
Part (b): moving pieces and multiple images

questions.q: Dev says, 'Both a pinhole camera and a plane mirror give upside-down images.' Do you agree? Explain.
questions.a: No. A pinhole camera gives an inverted (upside-down) image. A plane mirror gives an erect image with lateral inversion (left-right), which is not upside down.
s: Mirror image is laterally inverted, not upside down

questions.q: Write three clues about a device so that a friend can identify it as a periscope, including its parts, what it does and one place where it is used.
questions.a: Clues: it has two plane mirrors in a Z-shaped box; by reflection from both mirrors it lets us see objects not directly visible; it is used in submarines, tanks or by soldiers in bunkers.

questions.q: Meher wants to focus the image of a distant tree with her sliding pinhole camera. Describe what she does and what she will see.
questions.a: Point the pinhole towards the tree in bright sunlight, look through the open side of the smaller box with head and camera covered by a dark cloth, and move the smaller box forward or backward till the image appears on the tracing paper. The image will be upside down.
s: Pinhole faces distant object in bright sunlight
Slides the box to focus on tracing paper

questions.q: Radha says a kaleidoscope needs coloured bangle pieces to show any pattern at all. Mohan says that even with both ends left open and pointed at a tree it shows patterns. Decide who is right, explain what the three mirror strips do in each case, and say why a new pattern appears each time the tube is turned.
questions.a: Mohan is right: even with both ends open and pointed at a tree, one sees beautiful patterns, so the pieces are not essential. Radha is partly right that the pieces make coloured patterns. In both cases the three plane mirror strips form reflections of reflections, giving multiple images. Turning the tube changes what the mirrors reflect, so the pattern changes every time.
s: Radha partly right: pieces add colour

questions.q: Compare a pinhole camera, a periscope and a kaleidoscope: for each, give what is used inside, what we see, and what happens to the light.
questions.a: Pinhole camera: a tiny hole and a screen; we see an inverted image; light rays from the object pass through the tiny hole. Periscope: two plane mirrors in a Z-shaped box; we see objects not directly visible; light is reflected from both mirrors. Kaleidoscope: three plane mirror strips and coloured pieces; changing patterns; reflections of reflections make multiple images.
s: Pinhole: rays through the tiny hole
Kaleidoscope: multiple images from reflections of reflections

questions.q:
At a school science fair Group A shows a sliding pinhole camera, Group B a Z-shaped box with two plane mirrors, and Group C a tube with three mirror strips and coloured bangle pieces. On sports day the students want to watch the parade of the senior classes, which will pass behind a high wall at the edge of the ground.
(a) What is the nature of the image Group A's camera forms of a bright, distant object?
(b) Which group's device depends on reflections of reflections?
(c) What happens inside Group C's tube when it is turned?
(d) Which group's device should the students borrow to watch over the wall, and what would be the drawback of the other two?
questions.a: (a) Inverted (upside down). (b) Group C's. (c) The pieces move and the three mirrors form multiple images, giving a new pattern. (d) Group B's periscope: reflection from two mirrors shows what is not directly visible; the pinhole camera gives only an inverted image on a screen and needs bright light, and the kaleidoscope gives patterns, not a view.
s: Part (c): pieces move and multiple images
Part (d): periscope with drawbacks of the others

questions.q:
Ritu, a textile designer in Jaipur, is preparing a block print with two parts: a border of repeating geometric patterns and a central scene of the city skyline. She has three tools. Tool 1: a tube with three equal mirror strips joined in a triangle and coloured bangle pieces. Tool 2: a Z-shaped box with two plane mirrors. Tool 3: two sliding boxes with a tiny hole in one and tracing paper as the screen in the other.
(a) What would she see on the tracing paper if she pointed Tool 3 at the skyline in bright sunlight?
(b) What does Tool 2 let her do that she cannot do directly?
(c) Why does Tool 1 give so many different patterns?
(d) Which tool would you give her for the border and which for the skyline, and what must she remember when copying from the skyline tool?
questions.a: (a) An inverted (upside-down) image of the skyline. (b) See objects that are not directly visible, by reflection from the two mirrors. (c) Reflections of reflections in three mirrors make multiple images that change when it is turned. (d) Tool 1 for the border, since it gives ever-changing patterns; Tool 3 for the skyline, remembering that its image is upside down and must be turned the right way up when copied.
s: Part (b): sees hidden objects by reflection
Part (d): correct tool for each job with the inversion caution
